title: Uniqueness of the Philippines
seo_title: Grade 11 General Science: Uniqueness of the Philippines Worksheets (Strengthened SHS)
standard_code: Grade 11 General Science, Term 3: Earth and space science
standard_text: Uniqueness of the Philippines: an archipelago formed by plate tectonics in the Philippine Mobile Belt, its landforms, waters and mineral resources, its tropical climate and position in the typhoon belt, and its high biodiversity. (summary of the Strengthened Senior High School curriculum, General Science, Term 3)
meta_desc: Free Grade 11 General Science worksheets (Strengthened SHS curriculum, Term 3): the archipelago, plates and the Mobile Belt, landforms and waters, climate, and biodiversity. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: The Philippines lies between colliding plates.
key_sub: Its position makes it rich in resources and exposed to hazards.
body_html:
How to think about it

The Philippines is an archipelago of more than 7,600 islands. It lies between the Philippine Sea Plate and the Eurasian Plate, in the Philippine Mobile Belt, with trenches, active faults and volcanoes. This gives it mountains such as Mount Apo, fertile volcanic soils, and mineral deposits.

It is tropical and lies in the path of western Pacific typhoons. Its many islands isolated species, so it has very high biodiversity, including the Coral Triangle reefs. The same position that makes it rich also exposes it to earthquakes, eruptions, typhoons and floods.

Example

Which is the highest mountain in the Philippines?

In Mindanao

Answer: Mount Apo

Example

Why does the country have many endemic species?

Islands

Answer: islands isolated populations

Common mistakes

  • Thinking the Philippines is part of one stable plate.
  • Thinking the country has four seasons.
  • Thinking hazards and resources are unrelated.

faq.q: Why does the Philippines have rich gold and copper deposits?
faq.a: Volcanic activity and hot fluids concentrated metals in the crust.
A boundary separating Palawan's wildlife, linked to Borneo, from the rest of the Philippines.

items.q: A P wave travels 900 km at 8 km/s through the crust and upper mantle. How long does it take?
A P wave travels 360 km at 8 km/s through the crust and upper mantle. How long does it take?
Which deep feature lies east of Mindanao?
items.e: It is one of the deepest places in the ocean.

items.q: Which is the largest lake in the Philippines?
items.e: It supplies water and fish to many people.

items.q: A plate moves away from a mid-ocean ridge at 3 cm per year. How far from the ridge is rock that formed 8 million years ago? (100,000 cm = 1 km)
Seafloor spreads at 10 cm per year. About how old is rock 800 km from the ridge?
Why does the land heat up faster than the sea?
c: land has a higher specific heat capacity
water has a higher specific heat capacity and mixes, so the sea warms more slowly
items.e: This causes sea breezes.

items.q: Why is the Philippines an archipelago?
c: it is made up of many islands
items.e: Water separates the islands.

items.q: Which is the longest river in the Philippines?
items.e: It flows through northern Luzon.

items.q: Isabel finds seafloor rock 2,000 km from the East Pacific Rise that is 20 million years old. What is the average spreading rate? (1 km = 100,000 cm)
items.e: 2,000 km = 200,000,000 cm; ÷ 20 million years = 10 cm/yr.

items.q: A P wave travels 600 km at 6 km/s through the crust and upper mantle. How long does it take?
A P wave travels 240 km at 8 km/s through the crust and upper mantle. How long does it take?
Which is the highest mountain in the Philippines?
items.e: Mount Apo in Mindanao is about 2,954 m high.

items.q: Joy finds seafloor rock 50 km from the Mid-Atlantic Ridge that is 2 million years old. What is the average spreading rate? (1 km = 100,000 cm)
items.e: 50 km = 5,000,000 cm; ÷ 2 million years = 2.5 cm/yr.

items.q: Which gases are the main natural greenhouse gases?
c: water vapor, carbon dioxide and methane
items.e: N₂ and O₂ do not absorb infrared.

items.q: A plate moves away from the Mid-Atlantic Ridge at 1 cm per year. How far from the ridge is rock that formed 25 million years ago? (100,000 cm = 1 km)
A P wave travels 480 km at 8 km/s through the crust and upper mantle. How long does it take?
Diane finds seafloor rock 300 km from a mid-ocean ridge that is 10 million years old. What is the average spreading rate? (1 km = 100,000 cm)
items.e: 300 km = 30,000,000 cm; ÷ 10 million years = 3 cm/yr.

items.q: What happens to the surplus of energy at the tropics?
c: it is lost into space at once
winds and ocean currents carry it towards the poles
it is stored in the core
items.e: This drives global circulation.

items.q: About how many islands make up the Philippines?
items.e: The three main island groups are Luzon, Visayas and Mindanao.

items.q: Layer B has a seashell fossil. What does this tell you about the area when layer B formed?
c: The area was once dry land with plants or animals living on it.
The area was always covered by ice.
The area was once covered by ocean water.
The area has always looked the same.
items.e: A seashell fossil is evidence that the area was once covered by ocean water.

items.q: Why does the Philippines have very high biodiversity?
c: it has only one kind of habitat
it is tropical, has many islands that isolated species, and many habitats
it is far from the sea
items.e: Isolation on islands led to many endemic species.

items.q: Which of these is an igneous rock: chalk, mudstone, obsidian or slate?
items.e: Igneous rock is formed when hot, melted rock cools and hardens.

items.q: Is granite an igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic rock?
items.e: Igneous rock is formed when hot, melted rock cools and hardens.

items.q: Which line separates the plants and animals of Palawan and Borneo from the rest of the Philippines?
items.e: Palawan was once connected to Borneo.

items.q: Which of these is a metamorphic rock: basalt, granite, mudstone or slate?
items.e: Metamorphic rock is formed when other rocks are changed by great heat and pressure.

items.q: Which tool helps test a mineral's hardness?
c: a steel nail and a glass plate
items.e: Scratch tests compare hardness.

items.q: What is the streak of a mineral?
c: the color of its powder when rubbed on a tile
items.e: Streak can differ from the outside color.

items.q: Pyrite is gold-colored but leaves a greenish-black streak. Why is streak useful?
c: Streak shows how heavy a mineral is.
Streak is always the same as the outside color.
Streak can tell apart minerals that look alike.
items.e: Pyrite is called fool's gold.

items.q: Why is the Philippines exposed to many typhoons?
c: it is near the North Pole
it lies in the western Pacific, where typhoons form over warm water
it is in a desert belt
it has no ocean around it
items.e: About 20 tropical cyclones enter its area each year.

items.q: Layer A has a shark tooth fossil. What does this tell you about the area when layer A formed?
c: The area was once dry land with plants or animals living on it.
The area has always looked the same.
The area was once covered by ocean water.
The area was always covered by ice.
items.e: A shark tooth fossil is evidence that the area was once covered by ocean water.

items.q: Which describes the climate of the Philippines?
c: tropical, warm and humid, with dry and wet seasons
items.e: It lies between about 4° and 21° north of the equator.

items.q: Why are there rich mineral deposits in the Philippines?
c: the islands are made of ice
volcanic and plate activity formed deposits of gold, copper and nickel
the sea brought them every year
items.e: Magma and hot fluids concentrate metals.

items.q: Which underground river is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the New 7 Wonders of Nature?
items.e: It flows through a cave in Palawan.

items.q: Which of these is a sedimentary rock: basalt, chalk, granite or pumice?
items.e: Sedimentary rock is formed from layers of sand, mud or shells pressed together.

items.q: Which of these is a fossil: a crystal of quartz, a piece of brick, a seashell washed up today or a shark tooth found in chalk?
c: a shark tooth found in chalk
items.e: A fossil is the remains or trace of a living thing from long ago, preserved in rock.

items.q: Which mineral is the softest on the Mohs scale?
items.e: Talc can be scratched with a fingernail.

items.q: Layer B has a fern fossil. What does this tell you about the area when layer B formed?
c: The area was once covered by water.
The area has always looked the same.
The area was once dry land with plants or animals living on it.
The area was once covered by ocean water.
items.e: A fern fossil is evidence that the area was once dry land with plants or animals living on it.

items.q: What is the Chocolate Hills formation made of?
c: limestone hills shaped by weathering and erosion
items.e: There are more than 1,000 hills in Bohol.

items.q: What is the Coral Triangle?
c: a marine area with the world's highest coral diversity, including Philippine seas
items.e: The Verde Island Passage is called the center of marine shorefish biodiversity.

items.q: Which process turns loose sediment into sedimentary rock?
items.e: Minerals cement the grains together.

items.q: Which feature is most likely at a convergent boundary?
c: the Alpine Fault in New Zealand
the Southern Alps of New Zealand pushing up
a flat desert in the middle of a plate
items.e: convergent (plates move together): the Southern Alps of New Zealand pushing up.

items.q: What forms where an oceanic plate subducts beneath another plate?
c: a deep trench and a chain of volcanoes
items.e: The Pacific 'Ring of Fire' has many subduction zones.

items.q: How did Earth's layers form?
c: early Earth was hot enough to melt, so dense iron sank to form the core and lighter rock rose
they were all added by meteorites in order
the crust formed first and then the core
items.e: This separation is called differentiation.

items.q: Which kind of plate boundary forms deep ocean trenches?
c: no boundary: it is far from any plate edge
items.e: Convergent: plates collide. Divergent: plates separate. Transform: plates slide past.

items.q: Seafloor spreads at 1 cm per year. About how old is rock 400 km from the ridge?
Dennis finds seafloor rock 200 km from a mid-ocean ridge that is 5 million years old. What is the average spreading rate? (1 km = 100,000 cm)
items.e: 200 km = 20,000,000 cm; ÷ 5 million years = 4 cm/yr.

items.q: Seafloor spreads at 6 cm per year. About how old is rock 60 km from the ridge?
A plate moves away from the Mid-Atlantic Ridge at 1 cm per year. How far from the ridge is rock that formed 40 million years ago? (100,000 cm = 1 km)
About how old is Earth?
items.e: 13.8 billion years is the age of the universe.

items.q: Nico finds seafloor rock 300 km from the East Pacific Rise that is 5 million years old. What is the average spreading rate? (1 km = 100,000 cm)
items.e: 300 km = 30,000,000 cm; ÷ 5 million years = 6 cm/yr.

items.q: Kenneth finds seafloor rock 1,000 km from a mid-ocean ridge that is 25 million years old. What is the average spreading rate? (1 km = 100,000 cm)
items.e: 1,000 km = 100,000,000 cm; ÷ 25 million years = 4 cm/yr.

items.q: Which feature is most likely at a convergent boundary?
c: a flat desert in the middle of a plate
the Alpine Fault in New Zealand
items.e: convergent (plates move together): volcanoes along the Andes.

items.q: A plate moves away from the East Pacific Rise at 10 cm per year. How far from the ridge is rock that formed 50 million years ago? (100,000 cm = 1 km)
A plate moves away from the East Pacific Rise at 5 cm per year. How far from the ridge is rock that formed 5 million years ago? (100,000 cm = 1 km)
Which kind of plate boundary forms fold mountains such as the Himalayas?
c: no boundary: it is far from any plate edge
items.e: Convergent: plates collide. Divergent: plates separate. Transform: plates slide past.

items.q: How does a metamorphic rock form?
c: an existing rock is changed by heat and pressure without melting
items.e: Shale becomes slate; limestone becomes marble.

items.q: How does an igneous rock form?
c: by heat and pressure changing another rock without melting
by magma or lava cooling and crystallizing
by layers of sediment being cemented
items.e: Granite and basalt are igneous.

items.q: Seafloor spreads at 10 cm per year. About how old is rock 500 km from the ridge?
Seafloor spreads at 1 cm per year. About how old is rock 100 km from the ridge?
What is the amihan?
c: the northeast monsoon, a cooler, drier wind from about November to February
items.e: Amihan brings cooler weather to Luzon.

items.q: Where does most of Earth's internal heat come from?
c: radioactive decay of uranium, thorium and potassium, and heat left from Earth's formation
the Sun shining through the crust
items.e: It flows out at about 47 terawatts.

items.q: When is the rainy season in most of the Philippines?
c: the whole year with no change
items.e: The southwest monsoon brings rain.

items.q: Why is the Philippines warm even in December?
c: it is near the equator and receives strong sunlight all year
it is near the North Pole
it is far from the ocean
items.e: Places in the tropics are warm all year.

items.q: How does the greenhouse effect work?
c: greenhouse gases absorb infrared radiation from Earth's surface and re-emit some back down
items.e: Without it Earth would average about −18 °C.

items.q: What is a Hadley cell?
c: an ocean current along the Equator
a circulation in which warm air rises near the Equator and sinks near 30° latitude
items.e: There are Hadley, Ferrel and polar cells.

items.q: Which agency gives typhoon warnings in the Philippines?
items.e: PAGASA is the weather bureau of the Philippines.

items.q: What is the calm center of a typhoon called?
items.e: The eye has light winds and few clouds; the strongest winds are in the eyewall around it.

items.q: Why is the Philippines warm all year?
c: it is high above the clouds
it has more Moon than Sun
it is in the polar region
it is in the tropics, close to the equator
items.e: Sunlight hits the tropics almost straight down.

items.q: What is the habagat?
c: the southwest monsoon, a warm, moist wind that brings heavy rain
items.e: It blows from about June to September.

items.q: What is a typhoon?
c: a strong tropical cyclone with very strong winds and heavy rain
a strong earthquake under the sea
a cold wind from the north
items.e: Typhoons form over warm ocean water.

items.q: Why does a typhoon weaken when it moves over land?
c: it loses its supply of warm, moist air from the ocean
items.e: Typhoons get their energy from warm ocean water.

items.q: Why does a forest have a lower albedo than a desert?
c: dark leaves absorb more sunlight than pale sand
items.e: Clearing forests can change local climate.

items.q: Where do typhoons form?
items.e: Warm, moist air over the ocean gives the storm its energy.

items.q: What is Earth's energy budget?
c: the balance between incoming solar energy and outgoing reflected and infrared energy
the energy used by living things only
items.e: If more comes in than goes out, Earth warms.

items.q: What is latent heat's role in weather?
c: energy taken up in evaporation is released when water vapor condenses in clouds, powering storms
items.e: Tropical cyclones are fueled by latent heat.

items.q: What are the two main sources of energy for Earth processes?
c: solar radiation and Earth's internal heat
items.e: Internal heat drives plate tectonics; solar energy drives weather.

items.q: Where are the strongest winds of a typhoon?
c: in the eyewall, around the eye
items.e: The eyewall has the strongest winds and heaviest rain.

items.q: What is evaporation in the water cycle?
c: liquid water changing to water vapor, using energy from the Sun
items.e: Most evaporation is from the oceans.

items.q: What are the two seasons in the Philippines?
c: the dry season and the wet (rainy) season
a cold season and a hot season
a windy season and a calm season
items.e: PAGASA divides the year into dry and wet seasons.

items.q: Which huge, gentle fish can be seen in Donsol, Sorsogon?
items.e: It is the largest fish in the world and eats plankton.

items.q: What is ecosystem diversity?
c: the number of species in one quadrat
the variety of alleles in one species
the variety of habitats, communities and ecological processes in a region
the size of the largest ecosystem
items.e: A region with reef, mangrove and seagrass has high ecosystem diversity.

items.q: Which population is most at risk from a new disease?
c: a small, inbred population with low genetic diversity
a large population with many alleles
a population of a widespread species
items.e: Tasmanian devils have low genetic diversity, which helped facial tumor disease spread.

items.q: What is the main threat to the Philippine eagle?
items.e: Logging and clearing forests destroy its home.

items.q: Why is high genetic diversity important to a population?
c: it increases the population's size immediately
some individuals are more likely to survive a new disease or change
items.e: Variation is the raw material for natural selection.

items.q: Which tiny primate with very big eyes lives in Bohol?
items.e: Tarsiers are nocturnal and eat insects.

items.q: How do wildlife sanctuaries help endangered species?
c: they protect habitats where species can live and breed safely
items.e: Protected areas reduce threats.

items.q: Two sites each have 5 species. At site An each species has about 20 individuals; at site B one species has 90 and the rest have 2 or 3. Which is more diverse?
c: site B, because it has more individuals of one species
site B, because dominance means a healthier community
they are equally diverse because richness is the same
site A, because it has the same richness and higher evenness
items.e: Same richness, higher evenness = higher diversity.

items.q: Which is the national bird of the Philippines and is critically endangered?
items.e: Fewer than 400 pairs remain in the wild.

items.q: What is species diversity?
c: the number of species in an area and how evenly the individuals are spread among them
the variety of ecosystems in a region
the variety of alleles in a population
the number of individuals of one species
items.e: Species diversity takes in richness and evenness.

items.q: What does the 'rivet popper' hypothesis say?
c: losing species is like removing rivets from a plane: losing key ones can make the ecosystem collapse
items.e: Proposed by Paul Ehrlich.

items.q: What is genetic diversity?
c: the number of different species in an area
the variety of habitats in a region
the variety of alleles and genes within a species
the number of individuals in a population
items.e: Genetic diversity is variation inside one species.

items.q: What does 'critically endangered' mean?
c: a species has already died out
a species is at very high risk of becoming extinct in the wild
a species is found only in zoos
items.e: The IUCN Red List uses this category.

items.q: Which small wild buffalo is found only on Mindoro and is critically endangered?
items.e: The tamaraw is endemic to Mindoro.

items.q: Which sea mammal that eats seagrass is endangered in Philippine waters?
items.e: Dugongs need healthy seagrass beds.

items.q: Which is an ecosystem service of mangroves?
c: protecting coastlines from erosion and providing nurseries for fish
producing most of the oxygen for cities
items.e: Mangrove roots trap sediment and shelter young fish.

items.q: What does 'extinct' mean?
c: no living members of the species are left
the species moved to another country
items.e: Extinction is forever.

items.q: What does ‘ecosystem services’ mean?
c: money paid to visit a national park
the number of species in an ecosystem
the benefits people get from ecosystems, such as clean water, pollination and food
items.e: Mangroves protect coasts and act as fish nurseries.

items.q: What is species evenness?
c: the total biomass of the community
how similar the population sizes of the different species are
the number of individuals of the rarest species
items.e: A community where one species dominates has low evenness.

items.q: Which is a threat to sea turtles?
c: plastic waste, egg collecting and getting caught in fishing nets
items.e: Turtles mistake plastic bags for jellyfish.
